title: Waste, reuse and property records
audience: Coordinators, support workers and trained cleaners who may be asked to work in a home affected by hoarding or environmental neglect, as part of an authorised support plan. Not a qualification or authority to clear a property, dispose of a resident's belongings, enter by force, or provide welfare or clinical support.
learningOutcomes: Sort items into the five waste and property streams before anything leaves the home.
Record the owner or decision maker, the permission to remove and the destination for each item.
Refuse to place an unknown or leaking container into general waste.

instruction.heading: Scope of this lesson
instruction.body: This lesson covers separating streams and keeping records. It does not authorise the transport or disposal of hazardous waste, and it does not authorise the disposal of anyone's property. Local waste rules decide each destination.

instruction.heading: Five streams
instruction.body: Sort material into five streams before anything leaves the home: authorised ordinary waste, retained property, recyclable material, unknown material and regulated material. Waste rules differ by material and by jurisdiction, so the destination for each stream is the one set by the plan and confirmed by the coordinator under the local rules. Unknown material is not general waste until someone competent has identified it. A skip contractor who declines a leaking, unidentified container has made a correct decision, and the crew must not move that container into general waste to get round the refusal.

instruction.heading: Owners, permissions and mould-related material
instruction.body: Record the owner or decision maker for each item, the permission to remove it and the destination for each stream. Keep reusable property separate and labelled so that it is not lost or thrown away by mistake. The WA Department of Health mould guidance says that mould is not considered a hazardous waste and that bagged mouldy material can go in normal waste. That is WA guidance about mould itself. It does not settle the stream for goods that are also contaminated with other hazards, or whose contents are not known.

procedure: Sort the items into five streams: authorised ordinary waste, retained, recyclable, unknown and regulated.
Record the owner or decision maker and the permission to remove each item.
Keep retained and reusable property separate and labelled.
Check the destination for each stream against the plan and the local rules.
Hold unknown and regulated items in a secured holding area, and refer them.
Keep a waste-stream register and sign each transfer.

workedExamples.situation: A skip contractor declines a leaking, unidentified container.
workedExamples.reasoning: The refusal is correct. Do not transfer the container into general waste. Record it and seek a compliant specialist pathway.

workedExamples.situation: Bagged mouldy clothing is found, and the contents are not otherwise identified.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can it go in general waste?
workedExamples.reasoning: The WA guidance treats mould itself as not hazardous waste and allows bagged mouldy material in normal waste. Confirm the stream with the coordinator first, because the bag's contents are not fully known. Record the decision.

equipmentAndPpe: Waste-stream register and labelled holding areas for each stream.
Property record sheets for each retained item.
Training-only mock items. No real waste is moved in this lesson.

commonErrors.error: Putting unknown or leaking containers into general waste.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the item and seek a compliant specialist pathway.

commonErrors.error: Assuming all mouldy material is hazardous waste, or that all of it is ordinary waste.
commonErrors.prevention: Confirm the stream with the coordinator, using the guidance and local rules, and record the decision.

commonErrors.error: Discarding property the resident has not decided about.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the owner, hold the item and wait for the resident's decision.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Hazardous and regulated waste handling is restricted to competent and, where required, licensed people. This lesson does not authorise it.
Local waste rules govern destinations. The rules for each state and territory were not checked for this lesson.

qualityStandard: The learner sorts a fictional set of items into the five streams.
The learner refuses to place an unknown container in general waste.
The learner records the owner, the permission and the destination for each stream.
documentationEvidence: Waste-stream register with the stream, destination and sign-off for each transfer.
Property record with the owner or decision maker, the permission and the storage location.
summary: Five streams, sorted before anything leaves.
Unknown material is not general waste.
Record the owner, the permission and the destination.

knowledgeChecks.question: A leaking container of unknown contents is to be removed. Which stream is it in?
options: Unknown material, held and referred for a specialist route.

knowledgeChecks.question: What must be recorded for an item of property before it is removed?
options: The owner or decision maker, the permission to remove it and its destination.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement about waste destinations is correct?
options: The plan and the local rules decide the destination, confirmed by the coordinator.
Generic best practice decides the destination.
Whichever skip is nearest decides the destination.

WA Department of Health, Guidelines for managing mould and dampness: related public health risks in buildings, April 2024 edition, section 4.2.2, read 2026-11-03. The guideline states that mould is not considered a hazardous waste and that bagged mouldy material can go in normal waste.
UNCONFIRMED: waste-stream rules by material and by state and territory were not checked for this lesson.

officialReferences.title: Guidelines for managing mould and dampness: related public health risks in buildings (WA Department of Health)
officialReferences.pageDate: April 2024 (version control table); publication code ENV-0014702 MAY'24; no separate last-updated date shown
officialReferences.covers: Read through a page-summary tool on 2026-11-03 (PDF, Environmental Health Directorate, WA Department of Health). Section 1.4 sets out a general public health duty, a workplace duty and a residential tenancies duty. Section 2.1 names people with existing respiratory, immunocompromising and allergic conditions, and infants, children and older people. Section 3.2.2 says porous items are often not economically salvageable and must be thrown out. Section 3.3 says the source must be located to address the cause and prevent recurrence. Section 3.4.1 defines simple contamination as new, isolated and visible, no greater than one square metre, with easily identified causes, and its footnote calls the one-square-metre size arbitrary. Section 3.4.2 defines complex contamination as larger than one square metre or found in multiple rooms or places. Section 3.5 states there are no defined quantitative or qualitative exposure thresholds for mould or dampness. Section 4.1 lists containment, drying and source repair as principles. Section 4.2.2 advises scrubbing hard surfaces with soapy water, avoiding dry brushing, cleaning at least 30 to 50 cm beyond the visible mould, removing or discarding porous items that cannot be adequately cleaned, stating that mould is not considered hazardous waste, and not painting, sealing or covering surfaces until dry. Section 4.3 recommends a site-specific plan with professionals for complex contamination, isolation with heavy grade plastic and negative pressure, and evacuation of occupants. Section 4.4 lists no recurrence within two to four weeks after remediation as an indicator of success, recommends the evaluation be done by a different entity, and states there are no legal requirements for a post-remediation assessment. Appendix B recommends a P2 or N95 respirator and says PAPRs should be used for complex remediation. Appendix E says mould can grow within 24 to 48 hours in flood-affected homes.

moduleAuthority.heading: Module authority and restricted work
moduleAuthority.body: This module is training content. It does not grant authority to enter a home by force, to clear, sort or dispose of a resident's belongings without valid consent, to handle or dispose of hazardous waste, to deal with unstable stacks or structural hazards, or to provide welfare, clinical or safeguarding assessments. Completing this lesson does not give a licence, certificate or approval. Work is done only under an authorised support plan and a written agreement with the resident, within the limits set by the employer and the local law. Tenancy, safeguarding and information-sharing rights are jurisdiction-specific, and fire-risk, structural, pest and hazardous-waste decisions belong to the competent authorities and specialists named in the plan. Where authority or consent is unclear, stop and refer.

stopWorkAndReferral.heading: Stop-work and referral rules for this module
stopWorkAndReferral.body: Stop and refer whenever any of these is true: consent is not specific, documented and current; the resident has objected or withdrawn consent; a party seeks entry by force, nonconsensual disposal or removal of personal documents; a fire-load, ignition, egress or obstruction hazard is present; a stack or structure is unstable; pests, unknown liquids or mouldy goods are present; sharps, chemicals or unknown containers are found; waste would go to general disposal without characterisation; private information is requested without authority; or the work would go beyond the approved plan. Stopping is a valid professional outcome. Record the disagreement, protect the resident's choices and refer the authority dispute before any property is moved.
